Chapter 6. The Role of Human Agency: How Our Choices Shape Disease
As we build on the ideas of design and decay, let’s dive into something that’s both powerful and personal—the way our own choices shape the story of disease.
The natural world has its boundaries, sure. But when it comes to disease, what we do—both as individuals and as a society—can make things better or, sometimes, a whole lot worse.
Here’s the thing: we’re not just bystanders in the world of disease. Every single day, our actions—like how we farm, the way we build cities, how we handle hygiene, and the medical decisions we make—either help protect the balance of nature or, sometimes without meaning to, throw things off.
Take antibiotics, for example. When they’re handed out too easily, or used a lot in raising animals for food, we end up with bacteria that learn to survive those medicines. We’re not creating new life forms here. Instead, we’re encouraging the toughest, most resistant bacteria to stick around and spread.
That’s how we get this back-and-forth cycle—where our attempts to control disease can actually fuel it, making bacteria harder to treat over time.
Or look at how changing land—like cutting down forests or growing cities—brings us closer to wild animals. That opens the door for diseases to jump from animals to people, what we call zoonotic diseases. Again, we’re not making brand new germs. Instead, we’re making it easier for existing diseases to find new ways in.
So, what’s really going on here? There are a few big patterns worth paying attention to:
First, our influence is huge. The choices we make can disturb natural systems, sometimes letting new or more dangerous diseases take hold.
Second, there are feedback loops. Things like overusing antibiotics or changing habitats set up cycles where organisms keep adapting, and we keep chasing new ways to respond.
And third, there’s responsibility. Once we realize how much our actions matter, it calls for a new kind of stewardship—a commitment to act thoughtfully and with care.
Let’s make this real. Think about hospital-acquired infections. In places where lots of sick people are treated and antibiotics are common, bacteria can adapt fast, sometimes leading to tough outbreaks.
This isn’t evolution inventing something from scratch. It’s bacteria taking advantage of situations we’ve created.
So, here’s the key takeaway: stewardship really matters. We’re called to care for the world and its systems, respecting the way they’re designed and knowing their limits. And maybe most importantly, we need humility—because even the best intentions can have ripple effects we never saw coming.
